samples.text:
The table shows how many minutes people in four age groups spent on different media each day in one country in 2024.

Firstly, young people aged 16–24 spent the most time on video streaming, 185 minutes, and social media, 160 minutes. They only watched broadcast TV for 25 minutes and they listen to radio or podcasts for 40 minutes. They almost didn't read printed newspapers, only 2 minutes.

The 25–44 group used video streaming for 120 minutes and social media for 95 minutes. They spent 70 minutes on TV and 75 minutes on radio or podcasts, and newspapers was 6 minutes.

However, older people was very different. People aged 45–64 watched TV for 155 minutes and the 65+ group watched 270 minutes, it is the highest number in the table. They also listened more to radio or podcasts, 90 and 110 minutes, and read more newspapers, 18 and 42 minutes. But they used less streaming and social media, for example the oldest group spent only 20 and 15 minutes.

Overall, young people prefer new media and older people prefer traditional media like TV.
samples.why: Accurate data with a basic overview at the end · organised by age group so comparison is limited · simple, repetitive vocabulary · agreement, tense and word-order errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The table illustrates the average amount of time that people in four age groups in one country spent each day using five types of media in 2024.

Overall, there was a clear generational divide. Younger people spent most of their media time on video streaming and social media, while older age groups favoured more traditional media, particularly broadcast TV.

Among 16- to 24-year-olds, video streaming was the most popular activity, at 185 minutes a day, closely followed by social media at 160 minutes. Time spent on these two media declined steadily with age, falling to just 20 and 15 minutes respectively for those aged 65 and over. These were also the main media for the 25–44 age group, at 120 and 95 minutes.

The opposite trend can be seen for broadcast TV, radio and newspapers. Viewing of broadcast TV rose dramatically from only 25 minutes among the youngest group to 270 minutes, or four and a half hours, among the over-65s. Similarly, time spent listening to radio or podcasts increased from 40 to 110 minutes across the age groups. Printed newspapers were the least used medium overall, although reading time grew from 2 minutes for the youngest to 42 minutes for the oldest.
samples.why: Clear overview of the generational divide · trends across age groups presented logically · good range of cohesive devices · some less common vocabulary (favoured, medium) · frequent error-free sentences, one slightly awkward phrase.

samples.text:
The table compares the average daily time spent on five forms of media by four age groups in one country in 2024.

The dominant pattern is a sharp contrast between generations: streaming and social media account for most of young people's media time, whereas broadcast TV, radio and print become steadily more important with age. The oldest group spends more time on broadcast TV than any group spends on any other single medium.

The 16–24 age group devotes 185 minutes a day to video streaming and 160 minutes to social media, but only 25 minutes to broadcast TV and a negligible 2 minutes to newspapers. For those aged 25–44, streaming still leads at 120 minutes, but use is more evenly spread across social media (95), radio or podcasts (75) and TV (70).

Among older people, the picture is reversed. Broadcast TV accounts for 155 minutes a day among 45- to 64-year-olds and a remarkable 270 minutes among the over-65s, more than ten times the figure for the youngest group. Radio and podcasts follow the same upward trend, peaking at 110 minutes, as do printed newspapers, which occupy 42 minutes of the oldest group's day. In contrast, streaming and social media fall to just 20 and 15 minutes respectively for this group.
samples.why: Perceptive overview of opposing age trends · data selected and compared skilfully with an accurate multiple · cohesion natural and well controlled · precise vocabulary (negligible, devotes) · wide range of accurate structures.
